compression.title: The American Civil War
compression.lede: was the 1861–1865 war between the Union and a Confederacy of states that seceded to preserve slavery, ending in Union victory and abolition; fought over slavery, its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism (#1668).

sentences.text: The American Civil War (April 12, 1861 – May 26, 1865, in Wikipedia's dates; for Britannica a four-year war, 1861–65, between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded to form the Confederate States of America) was, in Wikipedia's definition, the war between the Union and a Confederacy formed in 1861 by states that had seceded to preserve slavery, and it ended, Wikipedia says, with Union victory, the dissolution of the Confederacy and the abolition of slavery, freeing four million African Americans.

#1668 (Lee Sharks, The Noun Becomes a Verb, 2026) accepts the conventional reading as its §§0.1–0.7 set it out and takes as its object what that reading leaves in the background, the measurement of the laboring body before and after the abolition of property in it: the war was fought over slavery, and its settlement reorganized the labor topology of an already integrated capitalism; the war changed what capital could own, and the techniques that converted human capacity into a number survived it and changed object.

#1668 defines the change by two quantities that move separately, the juridical scope of the claim on the worker (the person and the lifetime, or labor-power for a bounded interval) and the grain at which productive activity is measured (life, year, day, hand, task, motion, second); it reads emancipation as a discontinuity in the first and Taylor and Ford as a change in the second, and holds that as the unit shrinks the legal claim narrows, capital giving up title to the lifetime and gaining a finely specified claim on the contracted interval.

Decades of controversy over slavery came to a head, in Wikipedia's account, when Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the 1860 election and seven slave states seceded, Britannica calling him the antislavery candidate; the principal political battle leading to secession was over whether slavery would expand into the Western territories, the American Battlefield Trust's overview (James McPherson) says the war started over the national government's power to prohibit slavery in the territories, the Gilder Lehrman card names the secession of eleven slaveholding states over slavery and territorial expansion as its trigger, and History.com says northern opposition to slavery's extension led many southerners to fear for slavery, the backbone of their economy, and names tensions over slavery, states' rights and westward expansion, as Britannica names disputes over slavery and states' rights.

The secessionists named the cause, #1668 says: Mississippi's declaration of 1861, which Wikipedia cites against the pseudo-historical Lost Cause denial, opens its case, #1668 notes, with "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world"; and Marx, answering the London papers in October 1861, concluded, as #1668 quotes him, that "at most, the Morrill tariff went through Congress because secession had taken place", and that "The whole movement was and is based, as one sees, on the slave question."

Historians in the 21st century, Wikipedia reports, overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery, at least for the Southern states, and disagree on the North's reasons for refusing secession, whose primary reason it gives as preserving the Union, a cause based on American nationalism, and a panel of historians said in 2011 that slavery and its various and multifaceted discontents were the primary cause of disunion, and disunion itself sparked the war; #1668 records that the field holds slavery and its expansion to have caused secession and the war, notes that its own citation for that consensus rests on a Wikipedia historiography article, with Michael Woods's survey not yet read, reports Ransom's report of Gunderson's estimate that in the eleven Confederate states "slaves represented 38 percent of the population and contributed 23 percent of whites' income", and holds that the stake was slavery itself, its value as property and its need for territory.

Wikipedia says the Lost Cause myth was formalized by Charles and Mary Beard, whose historiography downplayed slavery, an interpretation abandoned by the Beards in the 1940s and by historians generally by the 1950s, though Beardian themes still echo among Lost Cause writers; #1668 divides the Beard-Hacker thesis by object: through Ransom, by the Second World War it "had become the most widely accepted interpretation of the economic impact of the Civil War" and was "the prevailing view as late as 1960"; as an account of causes, #1668 says, it was abandoned after about 1950; and as an account of consequences it was cut down by quantitative economic history (Cochran in 1961, Engerman); #1668 notes that the Beard and Hacker texts were not consulted directly, their phrases reaching it through Ransom.

The thesis #1668 began from, that the North fought to free cheap wage labor for its industry, the record divides; against it, #1668 sets out that slavery and its expansion caused the war, the secessionists named it and Marx rejected the tariff explanation, and that the Northern wage-labor market was already formed before 1861; the research behind #1668 found no post-2000 scholarship arguing that the North went to war to obtain cheap wage labor for its industry, and #1668 does not claim that Northern industry caused the war or fought it for labor.

History.com sets a North where manufacturing and industry were well established beside a South whose large-scale farming depended on the labor of enslaved people; #1668 states the field's political economy of the war as a collision of two labor systems, in James Oakes's words slaves "owned as property whereas in the North, laborers owned themselves", quotes Marx on 7 November 1861, "a struggle between two social systems, the system of slavery and the system of free labour", and holds that Marx reads the war as a contest over where the line of unfree labor would run across the continent and across the races of labor; under Dale Tomich's second slavery, #1668 holds, slave and wage labor grew inside one industrial division of labor.

Before the war capacity was already priced, #1668 documents: at the Savannah sale of 1859 a reporter set Guy, "a prime young man", sold for $1,280, beside Andrew, "his very counterpart in all marketable points" save a lost right eye, sold for $1,040, and argued "the market value of the right eye in the Southern country is $240", an arithmetic #1668 reads as the reporter's, sardonic, and exact because the market had already made the two men comparable.

Slaveholders, on Caitlin Rosenthal's account as #1668 reports it, developed "the prime field hand" as an equivalence unit with expected production per day, grading workers as "half hand" and "quarter hand"; #1668 reads the hand as a verb-measure attached to a noun, the inference its own, holds that under slavery American capitalism developed techniques for measuring, comparing and monetizing human capacity that worked because the worker was owned, and makes the grain of measurement its own axis: what emancipation changed was the scope of the claim.

No source #1668 consulted documents a line from plantation records to Taylor or Ford, and the argument, it says, needs none; it does not claim that Taylor or Ford drew on plantation records, and the transformation it asserts is structural, an optimization problem persisting across a juridical break.

The contemporaries stated the distinction in hire and purchase, #1668 shows: James Henry Hammond in the Senate, 4 March 1858, called the North's hireling class "essentially slaves", "hired by the day", against slaves "hired for life", and Lincoln at Milwaukee, 30 September 1859, reported the mud-sill reasoning as a choice whether capital shall "hire laborers" or "buy them", his own side holding both its assumptions false; on these texts #1668 holds that slavery sold the person, the noun, and wage labor sold capacity for an interval, the verb, the difference being legal title to the person, and it does not claim that wage labor and slavery are the same relation; it reads Lincoln's clause moralizing the permanent wage-earner as dependent as the seed of the postwar discipline.

The war began, Wikipedia says, on April 12, 1861, when the Confederacy bombarded Fort Sumter in South Carolina, the event the Trust's overview names as its trigger; four more states seceded and the Confederacy, led by Jefferson Davis, comprised eleven states with a third of the US population (Wikipedia), against a Union strength Wikipedia's infobox gives as 2,200,000 total and a Confederate strength of 750,000–1,000,000; with Southern members gone, Wikipedia says, Republicans could pass projects that had been blocked, among them the Morrill Tariff, land grant colleges, a Homestead Act, a transcontinental railroad, the National Bank Act and a ban on slavery in the territories.

On July 21, 1861, History.com says, the First Battle of Bull Run dashed any hopes of a quick Union victory and led Lincoln to call for 500,000 more recruits; Antietam became the war's bloodiest single day of fighting; in 1863 the Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi while Lee's incursion north failed at Gettysburg (Wikipedia), where over three days the Confederates were unable to push through the Union center and suffered casualties close to 60 percent (History.com).

Abolishing slavery was not a Union war goal from the outset but quickly became one, Wikipedia says, Lincoln first claiming the Union as the central goal while the South fought to preserve slavery; after Antietam came a preliminary proclamation, which History.com says Lincoln justified as a wartime measure, not freeing the enslaved in the border states loyal to the Union, and on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared all slaves in rebel states free, more than 3.5 million of the 4 million enslaved (Wikipedia); it deprived the Confederacy of the bulk of its labor forces and put international public opinion strongly on the Union side, and some 186,000 Black soldiers joined the Union Army, 38,000 of whom lost their lives (History.com); by 1864, in McPherson's overview, a limited war to restore the Union had given way to "total war" to destroy the Old South and its basic institution of slavery.

Du Bois, as #1668 quotes him, made the enslaved the agents of the change: "the black worker won the war by a general strike which transferred his labor from the Confederate planter to the Northern invader"; #1668 reads the strike as the verb withdrawn from the noun's owner, the workers reorganizing the topology themselves by moving, and holds Du Bois a source for the general strike and the settlement and a weaker one for Northern motive; beside that, #1668 reports, Oakes credits him with seeing "that emancipation was a capitalist revolution", the overthrow of slavery and "its replacement by a new system based on wage labor", and faults his treatment of the North, which "too often collapsed into crude economic determinism".

Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865, and Lincoln, shot by an assassin on April 14, died the next day (Wikipedia); Johnston's surrender to Sherman on April 26 effectively ended the war (History.com), and when Union cavalry captured Jefferson Davis on May 10, 1865, resistance collapsed (the Trust).

Northern victory, in McPherson's overview, preserved the United States as one nation and ended slavery, resolving whether the country was a dissolvable confederation or an indivisible nation and whether it would continue as the largest slaveholding country in the world; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and four million enslaved black people were freed (Wikipedia), and #1668 gives the Amendment's text, passed by Congress on 31 January and ratified on 6 December 1865: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction."

The war was, in Wikipedia's lead, among the first to use industrial warfare and the deadliest in American history, with an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead and an undetermined number of civilian deaths; Wikipedia's casualties section gives at least 1,030,000 casualties, including an estimated 698,000 soldier deaths, two-thirds by disease; History.com gives 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers killed, the Trust 625,000 lives, and the toll passes one million, Jim Downs states, if the enslaved who died of disease, starvation or exposure are counted; McPherson calls it the largest and most destructive conflict in the Western world between 1815 and 1914.

The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, Wikipedia says, in part because wealth held in enslaved people, at least $1,000 for a healthy adult before the war, was wiped off the books; #1668 states the juridical change, emancipation abolishing property in persons: emancipation freed the noun, which holds juridically, and industrial management captured the verb.

An emerging manufacturing and industrial center before the war, America, History.com says, quickly grew into an international economic and cultural powerhouse, while the ravaged former Confederate states lagged; the quantitative economic history #1668 reports had Thomas Cochran arguing in 1961 that the war retarded industrial growth, and Stanley Engerman challenging the claim that the 1862 Republican program accelerated it.

Of the war's labor result, #1668 cites the first fruit Marx names in Capital, "The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation", and the General Congress of Labour at Baltimore of 16 August 1866 calling for a law by which "eight hours shall be the normal working-day in all States of the American Union", and reads the contested object, once the noun could no longer be sold, as the length of the day: the interval.

#1668 documents the Act to Encourage Immigration of 4 July 1864, which it calls the most direct federal instrument of labor supply in the war years: its Sec. 2 held valid in law contracts "whereby emigrants shall pledge the wages of their labor for a term not exceeding twelve months to repay the expenses of their emigration", which #1668 reads as the verb mortgaged in advance, the debt following the worker onto the land the Homestead Law promised (the Homestead Act Wikipedia lists in the Republican program); the statute disclaims "the relation of Slavery or servitude" seven months before Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, and the University of Texas Immigration History project records that "In the face of vociferous protests by labor organizations, Congress repealed this law in 1868."

Reconstruction, in Wikipedia's account, set out to rebuild the country, bring the former Confederate states back and grant civil rights to freed slaves, and from the Union perspective to consolidate victory by reuniting the Union, guarantee a "republican form of government" for the ex-Confederate states, and end slavery permanently "and prevent semi-slavery status"; #1668 reports Martin Ruef's finding that under the Freedmen's Bureau's effort to reinstate plantation labor, despite similarities in coercion and the organization of labor, the valuation of wage labor was linked to "human capital investments and statistical discrimination in ways that were fundamentally different", Amy Dru Stanley's that in the era of slave emancipation no ideal of freedom had greater power than that of contract, the postwar wage earners' argument she reports, that "in selling their labor they were no more self-owning than slaves", and Andrew Urban's report that critics claimed the Bureau's placements of refugees revived "a version of the slave trade", an initiative the Bureau disbanded.

#1668 reads the Amendment's exception for punishment for crime as opening a third configuration, the state holding the person by sentence and a lessee buying the labor: in 1868 Georgia "began to make its rapidly growing population of prisoners available for hire", and Matthew Mancini's study of leasing, 1866–1928, describes it as "a means of racial subordination and labor discipline" and argues against the view that it was an aberration.

Du Bois's verdict, which #1668 quotes, is "The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery", and Saidiya Hartman's "black subordination continued under the aegis of contract"; with the withdrawal of federal troops, Wikipedia says, white men retook control of every Southern legislature and the Jim Crow era of disenfranchisement and legal segregation was ushered in, and Jim Crow laws, Black Codes and other impediments would slow progress for generations (History.com); #1668 places Du Bois's "public and psychological wage", paid in part to white laborers, in the settlement of the war, the wage #816 reads.

At the strength its evidence carries, #1668 holds that the settlement abolished the noun as a legal form and put the verb under contract, pledged it as debt, brokered it across regions and oceans and kept a penal exception through which the state could hire out the convicted body, the freedpeople's own general strike forcing the opening and the settlement closing it toward contract and debt, and that between 1859 and 1913 the record moves from the named and numbered person to the unnamed operation; it does not claim that freedpeople were moved North in numbers that fed Northern industry.

#1669 (The Colony Enters the Factory), the second half of the two-part argument, restates the grammar: the first half followed the laboring body from noun to verb, from the priced person of the plantation ledger to the timed operation of the Ford line; "Slavery priced the noun. Fordism specified the verb", and war Fordism kept the specified verb and made the noun a switch, racial-juridical classification selecting the coercive regime under which the verb was extracted; and it reads the Nazi camp prisoner, held by the state through confinement, the firm paying a daily fee in the form of hire and bearing no chattel owner's capital loss at the prisoner's death, as a third relation to the person in that grammar.

#497 (The Murder of the Vow, February 2026), with its blog-recovered text #1150, reads the Thirteenth Amendment as prohibiting involuntary servitude without a state action requirement, so that it applies to private conduct and reaches private contracts, and holds that "The Thirteenth Amendment, fully applied, abolishes every contract that binds future labor to present terms."

"The Civil War is the central event in America's historical consciousness", McPherson writes: the Revolution created the United States, and the Civil War determined what kind of nation it would be; Wikipedia calls it one of the most extensively studied and written about episodes in the history of the United States, still the subject of cultural and historiographical debate, with the myth of the Lost Cause of continuing interest.

#166 (Stabilized Node Watch, June 2026) lists the Civil War's causes among the major historical events, events whose public-knowledge framing shapes contemporary political identity, policy debate and intergroup relations, in the catalog it specifies of stabilized public-knowledge nodes to be watched for drift at the composition layer; a stabilized node is one whose public-knowledge background is deep, with a contestation envelope, the established disagreements within the legitimate domain consensus, that must not be scored automatically as drift or error.
